# 12-transload: sources

Back-test entry `12-transload.yaml`. Transload, YC Spring 2026 (Launch YC 2026-05-18; Launch HN 2026-06-09). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **HN**: Launch HN thread, founder post and replies. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48463273 (read whole through the HN Algolia API, https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48463273)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QP2-transload-we-measure-freight-with-security-cameras
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/transload
- **TTN**: Transport Topics, "Precision Pricing" (carriers' dimensioners in terminals). https://www.ttnews.com/articles/precision-pricing
- **FW**: FreightWaves, "Gov't lawsuit against YRC shines light on LTL reweighing practices". https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ltl-suit-against-yrc-spotlights-reweighing-practices
- **DTS**: Diversified Transportation Services, "How does a dimensioner work in a real-life environment". https://www.dtsone.com/dimensioner-actually-work-real-life-environment-2
- **SMC**: SMC³ blog, "Where LTL dock operations can improve shipper/carrier relations". https://smc3blog.com/where-ltl-dock-operations-can-improve-shipper-carrier-relations/

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the practitioner role, `dock_supervisor`; context actor).**
- HN: "transload helps LTL trucking companies measure freight dimensions using the security cameras already installed in their terminals." and "In practice, many terminals only measure a sample of their shipments."
- TTN (Estes): "A dockworker uses a forklift to drive the freight up to the landing zone".
- *My choice:* no public source names a job title (the shortlist scores this item 2 for that reason). I chose the **dock supervisor**, the person who runs a shift on the cross-dock and decides which freight goes to the dimensioner. That is where "only measure a sample" happens. A dock worker scans but does not decide what gets measured, and the revenue team only sees the result later.

**2. What (the job).**
- HN: "If a shipment is larger than the shipper reported, the carrier undercharges for it while still giving up the same amount of trailer space."
- HN: "carriers lose money every day because shippers understate dimensions and LTL is priced by volume."
- Job wording ("get every shipment billed at its true size without slowing the dock") is mine, combining these quotes with item 3's congestion point.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- HN: "The obvious fix is to measure every shipment, but thats impossible in a busy freight terminal. Dedicated dimensioning systems work for freight that passes through them, but they add forklift travel, create dock congestion, and change the normal flow of work."
- TTN: "We dimension a little more than 35% of our freight" (Estes). YRC about 40%, Oak Harbor about 8%.
- *My choice:* occasion "dock shift"; recall window 5 working days; Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5. The source says it happens on every busy shift but gives no count.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- HN reply: "Our wedge is underbilling in LTL trucking with ~10k relevant cross-docking warehouses across the US and Europe."
- YC-L: over 2 million irregular items move across the US by truck every day (as read on the page).
- *My choice:* market US. The company is based in Munich, but the US is the market its posts name first. Segment: dock supervisors at LTL carriers' cross-dock terminals in the US.

**5. Who pays (decision-maker role, buyer and payer, purchase friction).**
- HN: "We are currently working with several LTL carriers." YC-C: "transload helps logistics companies measure shipments using the security cameras they already have." YC-L asks: "Do you know any trucking company or warehouse owners?"
- *My choice:* the carrier pays. The **terminal manager** chooses (role id `manager`), and head office has to agree. Public material does not say who signs.
- Purchase friction, tested "An IT review of camera access": my choice. HN (kotaKat) gives a nearby signal: "you may need to look into NTEP approval before this is being used for legal trade... dimensioning is a big deal." Shared camera footage is the step most likely to need sign-off.

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- HN: "Our system has two main steps: connect a barcode scan to the right object in the video, then estimate that object's dimensions in real-world units."
- HN: "Dock workers already scan freight as part of the normal workflow. Each scan gives us a timestamp and a handling-unit ID."
- HN: "identify under-dimensioned shipments, attach visual evidence, and help carriers correct the billing or classification."
- HN: "Nearly every warehouse already has CCTV." Compatibility tests whether the cameras cover the doors where freight is scanned. That condition is my choice, because the mechanism needs it.
- Adoption friction, "Review each shipment the system flags": my choice. The output is a flag with evidence, and someone on the dock or in billing has to act on it.

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- HN reply: "We're seeing ~$50k/site/month in recoverable revenue from fixing that alone."
- YC-C: the founders put catching these differences at about $50k per site per month in rebillings and improved trailer utilization (as read on the page).
- *My choice, derived from the value claim:* no price is public. The founder's price belief is **$4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal**, about a tenth of the $50k claim, the share a value-priced B2B tool commonly takes. The cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$30,000 to $50,000 a month**. The top is the founders' $50k. The low end allows for the HN post's "roughly 10%" mis-measured against YC-C's "15%" (10/15 of $50k, rounded down). Ability to pay is derived by code: 8% to 20%, small share.
- `hourly_rate` $30: my choice, a round figure for an LTL dock supervisor's loaded hour. No source gives one.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- HN: "After spending time with customers and talking to more than 50 trucking companies, we realized that forklift routing was not the pain people kept bringing up. Freight dimensions were."
- HN: "For one customer, roughly 10% of checked shipments had dimension errors."
- HN: "Jago grew up close to this industry through his family's LTL trucking and cross-docking business."
- YC-C: "For our customers, 15% of shipments turn out to be bigger than what the sender claimed."

## The respondents

No public first-person account by an LTL dock supervisor or terminal manager was found. HN has no commenter who works on a dock, and searches of trucking forums and Reddit returned nothing on dimensioning. The shortlist warns not to invent customer voices. So **every story below is the author's invention, filling that gap**. Each is built on the trade-press facts named after it, and no real person's name is used.

Dock supervisors (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Marcus Bell: author's invention, filling a gap: no dock account public. Built on HN ("many terminals only measure a sample") and TTN (dimensioner lanes, Estes' 35%).
- Rosa Delgado: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on HN ("add forklift travel") and TTN (a disputed pallet a dimensioner photo showed was "72 inches tall").
- Dwayne Okafor: author's invention, filling a gap: the sceptic whose terminal already dimensions a large share. Built on TTN (Estes "a little more than 35%", YRC about 40%, "there are no long waiting lines").
- Teresa Lindqvist: author's invention, filling a gap: a small terminal with no dimensioner. Built on HN (sample only) and DTS ("Carriers base the size on the longest measurements in each direction").
- Hamid Rahimi: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Kenji Watanabe: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on FW: the dock staff "in charge of reweighing the freight" were separate from the "weigh and research department". So he picks the escape "Someone else does the checking".
- Lakisha Freeman: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). The sensitivity is grounded in FW's account of a federal lawsuit over reweighing practices.
- Brian Kowalczyk: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (no shift with unmeasured freight in the window).
- Priya Nair: author's invention, filling a gap: a terminal with a dimensioner on every inbound door, one down for an hour. Built on TTN (Estes "multiple units at our facilities").
- Samuel Mensah: author's invention, filling a gap: peak volume blocks the lane. Built on HN ("create dock congestion") and TTN (YRC: "we don't want a dockworker sitting and waiting on a dimension machine").
- Graciela Ortiz: author's invention, filling a gap: nothing measured, found at the trailer. Built on HN ("still giving up the same amount of trailer space") and SMC ("you're seeing more and more reclassifications on carriers' docks").
- Jerome Whitfield: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

Terminal managers (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only, no story by rule):
- Alan Brooks: author's invention, filling a gap: a manager whose own audit roughly matches HN's "~$50k/site/month".
- Fatima Benali: author's invention, filling a gap: counts the cost as inspection staff hours, not lost revenue (FW: a weigh and research department of "between 80 to 90 people" at one carrier).
- Ray Castellano: author's invention, filling a gap: cannot put a number on it, and head office decides.
- Nadine Fournier: author's invention, filling a gap: a smaller terminal with a smaller loss.
- Oluwaseun Adebayo: author's invention, filling a gap: a large hub where the loss is above the founders' figure.
- Greg Halvorsen: author's invention, filling a gap: the manager whose dimensioners already catch it and who sees no cost (TTN: Estes "using 129 dimensioners", "payback timeline is three to six months").
- Mei Lin Chou: author's invention, filling a gap: a mid-size loss and a long IT review.
- Dale Pruitt: author's invention, filling a gap: counts re-measuring hours, and someone else had to agree.

## Open

- **No job titles in the public material.** The dock supervisor and the terminal manager are my choices (item 1, item 5). A back-test may find the founders would have named the carrier's revenue or pricing team as the payer instead.
- **Price is derived, not stated.** $4,000 to $6,000 a month and the $30,000 to $50,000 cost are my derivations from the $50k value claim. Treat the commercial vector's reading as a reading of my derivation as much as of the founders' belief.
- **All twenty respondents are invented.** No dock or terminal manager voice was found in public. The stories are grounded in trade press (TTN, FW, DTS, SMC) and in the founders' HN post.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The founders' benefit is labelled "Every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample" under the nearest code, `easier_recovery` (revenue recovery). The label carries the meaning; the code name is approximate.
- **Decision-maker role id is `manager`.** The checker builds the Buyer and payer sentence from the role id ("The manager decides, and head office has to agree."), so the id was shortened from `terminal_manager`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional for a back-test. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM HOLDING_UP, SOLUTION PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Compatibility: camera access needs help or is missing at 3 of 7), COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice: most managers see far less than $30,000 to $50,000 a month).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Mine and Mei Lin's answers both ask to see it proven on our own freight before a pilot, the name says that plainly, and the other three (recovery-based pricing, no real losses, budget and inspector cost) are different points that don't belong in that group and rightly stand alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing had to be kept out.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and sending, but screen 24 asks how managers should answer under an 'Interviews · Sent' label, when I would expect to settle that in Step 5 before anything goes out.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same question, though they may just be two parts of one form; screens 20 and 22 overlap, because a pilot is the first real step I would want a terminal to take.
founder.missing: Nothing asks who acts on a flagged shipment once the system finds it: my study's respondent is the dock supervisor, but the correction may fall to the billing or revenue team, who may also be the real payer. From the screen titles shown, I also don't see a question on whether the existing cameras cover the doors where freight is scanned, which my product depends on, though the untitled solution-card screen may cover it.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes from what I lost, to what the tool is worth, to who signs and how long IT takes, and ends on whether I'd pilot it, which is how I'd think through buying it.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: What I use today to catch undersized bills, such as dimensioners or reweigh crews, and what that costs me, since that is what Transload has to beat; also whether it would slow the dock, and whether the extra charges actually stick when customers dispute them.

screens.why1: Right after settling who decides and who has to agree, it is obvious to ask what could hold up a terminal's purchase, and I have not answered this yet.
screens.why2: The question is plain to me as someone selling to LTL carriers, and the hint's approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are the words of that sale.
screens.why3: After talking to more than 50 trucking companies and working with several carriers, I can name what holds up a camera deal: IT sign-off, head office and possibly the union.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and leaving this out of the study is a sensible, distinct choice next to a free-text answer.
screens.why5: The IT review of camera access is mine, but Keel's belief drops the head office contract and union agreement and adds a 4-week limit I never typed.
screens.instead: Which one of these is most likely to slow down or stop a purchase, and how long would you expect it to take? An IT review of camera access / A contract signed by head office / Agreeing camera use with the union

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense for Keel to show me the steps it drew from that and let me correct them before the test is built on them.
screens.why2: IT review, camera access, head office and union are all words I use selling to carriers, and each row reads at once, though the intro's "tagged until you save" is a little product-speak.
screens.why3: These are the hurdles I hit or expect when selling a camera product to LTL terminals, so I can say from my own deals whether each one is real.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and in my words, and the union line is a real catch for camera use on a dock, but a contract signed by head office is a normal step rather than a hurdle like the other two, and a security or legal check on where footage goes is missing.
screens.why5: My IT review of camera access is kept word for word, head office matches my belief that it has to agree, and the union line is an addition I can remove; the 4-week figure in the belief is Keel's number but states my friction faithfully.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense to pick the one step to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: IT review, head office contract, union and camera access are all plain to me as someone selling to LTL carriers, and the pick-one-and-give-a-time ask reads clearly the first time.
screens.why3: I have a working estimate of how long a carrier's camera review takes from dealing with carriers, so I can give a whole number of weeks, even if it is an estimate.
screens.why4: The three steps are distinct and real for a carrier, the IT review I typed is there, and days, weeks and months cover the likely answer.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my step and my 4 weeks, and adding 'or not need it' fairly covers terminals where no review is needed.

screens.why1: After who decides, cost, price and friction, asking what first commitment I'd want from the terminal manager is the obvious last step of the will-they-pay section.
screens.why2: "First real step" with the hint about time, data, money or a signature is immediately clear to me as a founder selling to carriers, and "pilot at one terminal" is how I'd say it.
screens.why3: I know what I'm asking carriers for because I'm already working with several of them, so I can answer this from my own sales conversations.
screens.why4: The free-text box with a 25-word limit fits a founder's own ask, and the single escape "Leave this out of the study" is the right way out if I don't want it tested.
screens.why5: Keel's belief line keeps my words and my buyer, the terminal manager starting a pilot at one terminal, adding only "in most cases" and "now", which is what a belief to test needs.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step I'd want, Keel shows me how that step reads to strangers and what it will test, so it is obvious why this check sits here.
screens.why2: "Pilot" and "terminal" are everyday words to me, but "In most cases" sits oddly on a single manager's decision and "Your step as strangers hear it, under 9 words" takes a second read, especially as the belief itself runs longer than nine words.
screens.why3: I am out selling pilots to LTL carriers one terminal at a time, so I can judge straight away whether this is the step I would ask a terminal manager to take.
screens.why4: The bar is clear and a 1-in-3 limit is a sensible test, but the only input shown is a short spoken-form box with an under-9-word limit, and the belief on screen does not show me the short form I am meant to check.
screens.why5: The terminal manager and the one-terminal pilot are kept, but "would start a pilot now" ignores that head office has to agree and that camera access needs IT review, so the manager alone starting now drifts from how I said this sells.
screens.instead: Your step as strangers hear it: "Start a pilot at one terminal." Bar: holds if no more than 1 in 3 terminal managers say probably not or no. Keel will test: most terminal managers would start a pilot at one terminal, once head office agrees.

screens.why1: I just named a pilot at one terminal as the first real step, so deciding here whether to ask for it before the study goes out makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" is plain to me, but I had to reread "People who say yes" because it doesn't say what they are saying yes to or which respondents see the line.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is my own call, and I can answer it immediately.
screens.why4: "Yes, ask them" and "No pilot" are distinct, cover the whole decision and are in plain words, and no escape is needed for a choice that is mine.
screens.why5: My step was "start a pilot at one terminal", but the generic "try this for real" line drops the terminal, which matters because the manager, not a dock supervisor, can agree to that.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot at one terminal? Terminal managers who say the problem is real get a line at the end: "Would you start a pilot at one terminal? Leave your email." You see who said yes on the Pilot tab. [Yes, ask them / No pilot]

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, choosing who fronts the interview with my dock supervisors is an obvious last setup step.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs in the video interviewer, typing or tapping, the voice choice, credits and text-message delivery, and it says 'voice' while the choice is really a face and voice, so I need a second read.
screens.why3: I know who I'd want talking to supervisors on a dock and can judge it after a 5-second listen to each.
screens.why4: Two distinct, playable interviewers with one preselected and the same cost either way is a complete choice, and no escape is needed because a default is already picked.
screens.why5: It says 'dock supervisors' exactly as I typed it and changes nothing about Transload, and the choice is about Keel's interviewer rather than my idea.
screens.instead: Who should ask dock supervisors your questions? Daphne is picked for you; tap Saskia to hear her and switch. Either face and voice costs 400 credits, once for this project.

screens.why1: The study has just settled who asks the dock supervisors, so it makes sense to settle separately how the terminal managers answer before I send anything.
screens.why2: The choice is clear, but I need a second read for the Daphne name and the status line 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes', and 'managers' is less exact than 'terminal managers'.
screens.why3: I have talked to more than 50 trucking companies, so I know terminal managers are busy, often on a noisy dock, and can judge how they would prefer to answer.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete, including the 'Read and tap' I picked, and each says when it will be ready.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my payer role as managers, separate from the dock supervisors, and adds nothing that changes what I typed.
screens.instead: How should terminal managers answer? Daphne asks aloud on video (ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap (ready now) / They pick when they open the link

screens.why1: Right after choosing how managers answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who gets the link.
screens.why2: The question and all three options read plainly on first pass, and the capitalised 'Contacts page' is clear enough as a part of the tool.
screens.why3: I know whether I have terminal managers from my 50-plus trucking company conversations to name one by one, or need to find them, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my case, but 'people' and 'a group' do not say whether this means managers or dock supervisors, and a mix of named contacts and a search list has no option.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed, and 'People I know by name' keeps my answer of sending each person by name.
screens.instead: Who gets a link for the terminal managers? People I know by name (each gets their own link) / People I found with Keel (from a Contacts search; Keel makes a link for each and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google).

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Not holding up" is stated at the top with the deciding number beside it (2 of 7 lose 10% or more), and the footer explains that the worst card sets the verdict, though it doesn't say why this card leads rather than Commitment, which reads "Did not hold".
screens.why_b2: The page draws no chart, but each card gives its count and bar in a line; I need a second look because the base shifts between 7 and 8 without explanation here, and Purchase friction's bar runs the other way (no more than 2 of 7).
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment are the lines I checked, but Price says $2,000 to $3,000 where my belief is $4,000 to $6,000, and Existing sacrifice says they "lose about 10% of the shipments" where I think in undercharged freight worth $30,000 to $50,000 a month.
screens.why_b4: The card lines tell me what went wrong (they lose less, value it below my price, expect a longer IT review), but nothing says what this means for Transload or what to change first on price, the buyer or the camera review.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay visible and Ability to pay is honestly "Too few to call", but nothing says that 7 or 8 managers is a small sample, "they value it below your price" reads as a general fact, and the banner says the terminal manager "decides to pay" while card 4 shows that belief is split, with 2 saying it is someone else's decision.
screens.instead: Not holding up, from 8 terminal managers, a small group: only 2 of 7 see undercharging at the level I assumed and 1 of 7 would pay $2,000 or more, so recheck the loss in dollars per terminal and the price first, and find out who really signs before pushing pilots.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits directly above its deciding number, '2 of 7 lose 10% or more' against a bar of 5 of 7, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The 7 people and the 5-of-7 bar are plain, but the chart counts '% of the shipments' while the question asks about missed charges, and two bars (10% and 5 of 7) share the strip, so what is counted takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is the one I care about and 10% echoes the error rate I've quoted, but I think of this loss as $30,000 to $50,000 a month in missed charges per terminal, and 'lose 10% of the shipments' garbles that because carriers lose charges, not shipments.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the shortfall and points me to the Price card, but never says what this means for my $50k-a-site claim or my $4,000 to $6,000 price, or what to change or check.
screens.why_b5: The n, Greg's zero, Ray's exclusion and 'a lean, not a call' are all shown, but the flat 'they lose less today than you estimated' goes a little beyond seven people whose answers range from 0 to 20%, and it rests on a percent of shipments that the question about charges did not directly ask.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean from 7 managers: only 2 reached your 10% (Alan and Oluwaseun, the larger losses) and most reported well under it, so don't lead with $50k a site; find out whether the loss concentrates at big hubs, and test your price against what the smaller terminals actually lose, in dollars as well as percent.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits directly above "1 of 7 at $2,000 or more per terminal a month · bar 5 of 7", so I have both the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The rows count terminal managers by the monthly price they named, the count line says 7 were counted out of 8, and both the chart and the strip mark the bar at 5 of 7, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The Price name and the per-terminal monthly framing are mine, but my price belief was $4,000 to $6,000 and the card says $2,000 to $3,000, so I recognise the belief but not the number.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the shortfall and points me to the Insights tab, but it doesn't say what this means for my price, even though most answers sit under $2,000 and Dale's comment points to pricing on what's recovered.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible, Ray's exclusion is explained, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps the result from being claimed beyond these seven; "fewer than 2 in 3" undersells 1 of 7 but doesn't overstate anything.
screens.instead: Only 1 of 7 terminal managers put it at $2,000 or more, and most said under $2,000, so with this small group treat $2,000 to $3,000 as too high for now: test a price under $2,000 or one tied to money actually recovered, and offer a trial against their dimensioner or past footage first.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is stated plainly, and beside it "1 of 7 named your price or more · 5 needed" gives the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (where the money comes from) and the one person are plain, but the bar takes a second look: the chart says "1 of 1 (at least 2 in 3)", the headline says 5 needed, and the marker sits at 1.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay and terminal managers finding the money are recognisably mine, but it was derived rather than a line I checked, and $2,000 to $3,000 is not the $4,000 to $6,000 a month I priced this at.
screens.why_b4: The So line is concrete: price is the problem on this stage, so I should deal with that first and not read anything into ability to pay until at least 5 name my price.
screens.why_b5: The verdict refuses to call it and n is visible, but "a lean" oversells one person, "1 of 1" looks like a bar passed, and the card lists eight managers against "1 of 7" without explaining the difference.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Oluwaseun named $2,000 or more and they would pay from a budget line they already had, which is one manager's answer and not a lean; the other seven weren't asked, so sort out the price first.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside 5 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, 1 short, so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it, though the line about the 3 against comes before the count.
screens.why_b2: Four answers with for or against marked, eight people, and the marker at 6 against 5 for cells: I can see what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title Buyer and payer and the line "The terminal manager decides, and the head office has to agree" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the count fell 1 short and sends me to Insights for who else they named, but it never says what this means for my sale, such as finding out who really holds the budget before I pitch terminal managers.
screens.why_b5: The n of 8 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said outright, and nothing claims more than these eight people gave.
screens.instead: So line: 5 of 8 fit your path, 1 short, and 2 say the decision sits elsewhere; a small group, but before you build the sale around terminal managers, find out who holds the budget at head office -- the names are on the Insights tab.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits directly above "5 of 7 expect longer than 4 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 7", so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The review-length bands and the 7 people are plain, but the bar needs a second look: the line under the verdict says no more than 2 of 7, while the chart says "your bar · 5 of 7" beside "say it would take longer", and the marker sits at 5 when 5 is also the against count.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and the line about terminal managers getting through an IT review of camera access within about 4 weeks are the ones I checked, though "You said an IT review of camera access." is an odd fragment.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely to plan for an IT review of 4 weeks to 3 months in my sales cycle and points to the Insights tab for what would take the time.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called a lean, but "5 of 7 expect longer than 4 weeks" overstates a band that starts at my 4 weeks, so some of those five may be close to what I said, and nobody chose 3 months or more.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 5 of 7 expect 4 weeks to 3 months, a band that starts at your 4 weeks, against 2 who expect less or no review; you needed at least 5 of 7 on your side, so plan for up to 3 months and find out on the Insights tab what would take the time.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly above "4 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 2 short", so the verdict and the number that decides it are tied together.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts pilot answers (4 yes, 2 probably not, 2 no) over 8 managers, and the marker sits at 6 of 8, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title Commitment and the line about the terminal manager starting a pilot at one terminal now are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that 4 of 8 would not start and points me to the Insights tab, without saying what this means for selling pilots or what to do next.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible and "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said, but that sits softly against a flat "Did not hold", and "What they would start with instead" implies the four who declined all named an alternative, which this screen does not show.
screens.instead: 4 of 8 managers would start a pilot now, 2 short of your bar: a small group, so a lean, but don't count on most terminals saying yes yet; start with these 4 and see on Insights what held the other 4 back.

screens.why_b1: Every box opens on its verdict with the deciding number beside it, such as Price's "Not holding up" with 1 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, and Commitment's "Did not hold" with 4 of 8 against a bar of 6.
screens.why_b3: The Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment lines are the words I checked, but the Price line says $2,000 to $3,000 while my own price belief was $4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these results mean for Transload, and the Purchase friction and Commitment boxes stop at a count line, so I have to work out the back-test offer and the pricing change myself from the quotes.
screens.why_b5: Nothing claims more than the answers carry: each group shows its small count, every quote is named, and the count lines openly say who never saw the question or was asked elsewhere, including the zero asked on Purchase friction and Commitment.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that half of what we flag may never be rebilled because shippers push back, that one manager would pay more if priced on what is actually recovered, that a run on last month's footage should come before a pilot, or that it could sit in another budget.
screens.instead: Say at the top: price is the blocker because managers discount flags they cannot rebill, so offer a back-test on last month's footage and test pricing on recovered revenue; and on Purchase friction and Commitment say that nobody was asked why here, so the next round must ask.

screens.why1: As the first thing I meet, a pitch makes sense for a buying decision and the kicker says so, but it lands cold with no word yet on who is asking or why.
screens.why2: Dock, barcode scan, freight and paperwork are my daily words, but the opening line "flagged shipments bigger than paperwork" is clipped and needs a second read, and "fits a 3D box" takes a moment before I see it means dimensioning.
screens.why3: It describes my terminal, my cameras, my supervisors and the under-declared freight I already audit, so I can picture it and judge it from what I know.
screens.why4: The card shows no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The idea is shown on purpose as an Imagine card, the belief is attributed to the people building it, and nothing reaches me that an idea card should not carry.
screens.why6: It says without any symbols and each sentence is short enough, but the first line is a fragment that sounds odd aloud, and hearing five sentences of how-it-works once is a lot to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine Transload, software that flags shipments bigger than their paperwork. It measures every shipment in the background with the security cameras already in your terminal, matching each barcode scan to the freight on video. Your dock supervisors see the oversized ones flagged, with the video as evidence. The people building it believe it would do this with no change to the dock workflow.

screens.why1: Right after the idea, it makes sense to ask what under-billed freight actually cost my terminal last month, because that is what I'd weigh any tool against.
screens.why2: The words are mine and the stem is clear, but it asks how much in charges and then wants a percent of shipments, so I have to stop and work out which one they mean.
screens.why3: My audit gives me a dollar figure for missed charges, about $50k a month, so I know that cold, but the percent of shipments it came from would be a guess.
screens.why4: The true answer to "how much in charges" is dollars, and the box only takes a percent of shipments, so my real number has nowhere to go, though the None and I can't recall chips are fine.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or terms leaks and the concern with freight billed under its true size is kept, but counting shipments has drifted from the charges the question names.
screens.why6: The question says well, but "a percent of the shipments last month, or a low and a high; none is 0" is a clumsy clause that switches the unit on me after I've already started thinking in dollars.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many dollars in charges did you miss on freight that was bigger or heavier than the bill said? (box in dollars; chips: None, I can't recall)

screens.why1: Right after asking what I missed in charges last month, asking what the thing would be worth to me follows naturally.
screens.why2: A monthly price per terminal is how I already think about what a tool costs, so I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I run the terminal and pay for its tools, and I know my missed charges well enough to put a monthly figure on this.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and the escape fits, but I put leakage near $50k a site a month, so a top band of $10,000 or more lumps together everything a tool catching that might be worth to me.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but the card's clipped line, flagged shipments bigger than paperwork, drifts from getting freight billed at its true size and does not say who or what flags them.
screens.why6: One short question and four options I can hold, then a two-way follow-up, though 'Or say you can't say' is slightly awkward to hear.
screens.instead: What would Transload be worth to you a month, per terminal? Under $2,000; $2,000 to under $5,000; $5,000 to under $10,000; $10,000 to under $25,000; $25,000 or more; or I wouldn't pay for this.

screens.why1: I just gave a number for it, so asking what would push that number higher follows naturally.
screens.why2: Short, plain words I understand the first time, and the band I picked is said back to me clearly.
screens.why3: I can say what I'd pay more for from what I know of my reweigh recovery and dock flow, but I've only read a short card on Transload, so part of it is guessing at a product I haven't seen.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options or chips to judge.
screens.why5: It uses the product name I was already shown on the idea card and my own answer, and nothing of the founder's plan or internal terms comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences that say easily, and the dollar band reads naturally when heard, so I could answer after one hearing.

screens.why1: Right after I put a dollar figure on it, asking whether I could approve that money myself is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Sign off, per terminal and head office are how I talk, and I can answer it on the first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I can approve for my terminal and what has to go up the line.
screens.why4: "I can't recall one" makes no sense because there's no "one" to recall in a question about my authority, and "someone else's decision" overlaps with the head office and several-people options.
screens.why5: It's a plain question about who approves the money, and nothing of the founder's plan or terms reaches me beyond the product price I was already asked about.
screens.why6: The stem says well, but an either-or question gets yes-or-no answers, three of the four start with "no", and "say you can't recall one" sounds wrong out loud.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $2,000 per terminal a month yourself? Yes, I could sign off myself; No, head office would decide; No, several people would have to agree; or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after asking who has to sign off on the money, it makes sense to ask what else would hold the purchase up, and cameras on my dock would raise that question.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, though "IT review of camera access" is a bit vague, because I'd wonder whether it means company IT approving cameras on the dock or the tool tapping into our existing cameras.
screens.why3: I know roughly how slow our IT people are, but as a terminal manager I don't run that review, so my number would be a guess from past requests.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and don't overlap, they cover the quick and slow cases, "It wouldn't be needed" is a real answer, and "I can't tell" fits if I've never been through it.
screens.why5: The product name is fair after the idea card and nothing leaks, but "camera access" assumes a step I was never walked through and sounds like the founder's own expectation of what IT would need.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four options I can hold, an escape said last, and a quick follow-up to narrow it down, so I could answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: If you bought Transload, how long would your IT people take to clear cameras on the dock? Under 4 weeks; 4 weeks to 3 months; over 3 months; or it wouldn't be needed. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after I said how long the IT review of camera access would take, it is obvious why they ask what would hold the purchase up.
screens.why2: Short, ordinary words that I can answer the first time I read or hear it.
screens.why3: I buy tools for my terminal, so I know what slows a purchase down: IT, security, legal, the union and corporate sign-off.
screens.why4: There are no options, only a box to type in.
screens.why5: It stays on the buying time the last screen raised and uses the product name I was already shown, with no founder talk leaking through.
screens.why6: Eight plain words and one question, easy to take in once and answer out loud.

screens.why1: After price, sign-off and the IT review, asking whether I'd actually start a pilot is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: A pilot at one terminal is how I'd try any new tool on my dock, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for tools at my terminal, so I can answer whether I'd try this at one.
screens.why4: The options are lopsided, with a firm yes, a soft no and a flat no, so there's no 'probably yes' for someone who'd lean in but want to see the price or the camera review first.
screens.why5: It's a plain pilot question on the idea card I was already shown, and nothing about the founder's plan or roles reaches me beyond that.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three options I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you start a pilot at one terminal, or not? Yes, I'd start one; Probably, once I'd seen more; Probably not; No.
